report.title: Your Later-Life Retirement Income
report.rawMarkdown:
# Your later-life retirement income looks strong

Once the main pensions are in payment, illustrative gross household pension income is approximately €77,500 a year before relying on the known €267,000 of DC pension savings or the spouse's DC pension. Current household expenditure is approximately €42,000 a year excluding the mortgage. The mortgage currently costs €11,352 a year and has 109 months remaining, so it is expected to finish before the full later-life pension picture is in place.

The later-life income estimate comprises approximately €27,840 from the UK Defined Benefit pension, €14,555 from the client's UK State Pension, €14,555 from the spouse's UK State Pension, illustrative Irish State Pensions of €4,669 and €3,891, and approximately €12,000 from the foreign life-savings or insurance product. The UK amounts use an illustrative exchange rate of £1 = €1.16.

The €77,500 figure is gross income, while €42,000 is current household spending, so the approximately €35,500 difference is not a net disposable surplus. Tax residence, particularly a possible move to Spain, will affect the eventual net-income comparison.

The household also has €267,000 of known DC pension assets, comprising €143,000 with Irish Life and €124,000 with New Ireland. The spouse also has a DC pension whose current value is not yet known.

The key planning question therefore shifts from later-life income adequacy toward the retirement bridge: how soon work can stop and how the period before the major pensions commence can be funded.

modules.title: Retirement Bridge - Could You Retire at 57?

generated.summaryHtml: The model suggests there is a credible route to retiring at approximately 57 and bridging the period until your later-life pensions take over. Under the assumptions modelled, there is no unfunded shortfall, your €106,704 two-year cash reserve is never needed, and your €200,000 foreign property does not need to be sold. Start with the headline result, then follow the timeline to see how the tax-free lump sum, accessible investments and progressively commencing pension income work together through the bridge.

report.title: Could You Afford to Retire at 57?
report.rawMarkdown:
# Could you afford to retire at 57?

Your longer-term retirement income looks strong, but most of that income does not arrive immediately. The question is therefore whether your existing assets and pension can bridge the period from retirement at 57 until your later pensions begin. The model uses deliberately cautious assumptions and produces no unfunded shortfall. It does this without selling your €200,000 foreign property and without drawing on the protected €106,704 two-year cash reserve.

blocks.title: What the result means
blocks.markdown: On the assumptions modelled, retiring at approximately 57 appears financially achievable within this retirement bridge. Your early retirement is initially funded from the tax-free pension lump sum and accessible investments. As your spouse's pensions, your retirement-fund withdrawals and eventually your own major pensions begin, the amount required from accessible investments falls until pension income takes over.

blocks.title: Why this is deliberately a difficult test

items.title: No extra non-pension savings
items.markdown: The model assumes you save nothing further outside your pension during the next three working years, even though your current finances may allow additional saving.

items.title: Company shares receive a severe tax haircut
items.markdown: The model assumes virtually the entire €220,000 company-share value is exposed to 33% CGT after a €1,270 exemption, leaving €147,819 of net sale proceeds. This is a stress assumption, not an estimate of your actual CGT liability. Your actual base cost needs to be established.

items.title: Cash earns nothing
items.markdown: The €106,704 protected cash reserve is assumed to earn 0% throughout the model.

items.title: Investment growth is modelled smoothly
items.markdown: The accessible portfolio and pension are modelled using 5% annual growth. Real investment returns will be uneven, and poor returns early in retirement could materially change the result.

items.title: Pension taxation is simplified
items.markdown: The model applies a simplified 30% effective tax rate to taxable pension income and retirement-fund withdrawals. Actual taxation will depend on your income and future tax residence, including whether you retire in Ireland or Spain.

items.title: Spending continues to rise
items.markdown: Non-mortgage household expenditure increases by 2% each year. Your spouse is also assumed to stop working when you retire, so there is no employment income for either of you after age 57.

blocks.title: The bigger picture
blocks.markdown: The three additional working years are doing more than simply delaying retirement. They allow your pension to grow, add three further years of substantial pension contributions and move you materially closer to the point where your spouse's and then your own pension income begins. The result is a potential retirement at 57 where your existing assets need to fund a temporary bridge rather than support the household indefinitely.
bullets: Your later pension income takes over before the bridge assets are exhausted.

The foreign property is not required.
The next question is how much additional safety margin you would want before actually retiring.
